```text
1	# Editing `index.html` in VS Code, deploying to `gs://emores` via GitHub
2	
3	**End result:** you open the folder in VS Code, edit `index.html`, hit commit + push,
4	and ~30 seconds later the file on your bucket is updated. No console clicking, no drag-and-drop.
5	
6	You only do steps 1–5 once. After that, only step 6 matters.
7	
8	---
9	
10	## Step 1 — Get the current `index.html` onto your computer
11	
12	In the Cloud Storage browser tab you have open:
13	
14	1. Find the `index.html` row.
15	2. Click the **⋮** menu at the far right of that row → **Download** (*Pobierz*).
16	3. Save it somewhere sensible, e.g. `Documents/emores-site/`.
17	
18	Do this *before* anything else — the copy in the bucket is the source of truth right now,
19	and you don't want to overwrite it with an older version later.
20	
21	## Step 2 — Set up the local folder
22	
23	Unzip `emores-site.zip` (the scaffold I sent) into the same place, so you end up with:
24	
25	```
26	emores-site/
27	├── index.html                    <- the file you downloaded in step 1
28	├── .gitignore
29	├── SETUP.md
30	└── .github/
31	    └── workflows/
32	        └── deploy.yml
33	```
34	
35	Then, in a terminal:
36	
37	```bash
38	cd path/to/emores-site
39	git init -b main
40	git add .
41	git commit -m "Initial commit: index.html from gs://emores"
42	```
43	
44	> The `.github` folder starts with a dot, so it's hidden in Finder/Explorer.
45	> It will show up fine in VS Code.
46	
47	## Step 3 — Create the GitHub repo and push
48	
49	1. Go to <https://github.cogit remote add origin https://github.com/m/new>.
50	2. Name it `emores-site`. Set it to **Private** (recommended — it's your live site's source).
51	3. **Do not** tick "Add a README", "Add .gitignore", or "Choose a license". You need an empty repo.
52	4. Click **Create repository**, then run (swap in your username):
53	
54	```bash
55	git remote add origin https://github.com/YOUR-USERNAME/emores-site.git
56	git push -u origin main
57	```
58	
59	If Git asks for a password, it wants a **personal access token**, not your account password —
60	easiest fix is to let VS Code handle it: open the folder in VS Code, click the Source Control
61	icon in the left bar, and use **Publish Branch**, which signs you in through the browser.
62	
63	## Step 4 — Create a service account so GitHub can write to your bucket
64	
65	This is the "key" GitHub uses to upload. It is scoped to *only this bucket*.
66	
67	**4a. Create the account**
68	
69	1. Console → **IAM & Admin** → **Service Accounts** → **Create service account**.
70	2. Name: `github-deploy`. Click **Create and continue**, then **Skip** the optional role step
71	   (you'll grant the role on the bucket instead, which is tighter), then **Done**.
72	3. Copy the email it generated — it looks like
73	   `github-deploy@project-4010577e-246a-46aa-be6.iam.gserviceaccount.com`.
74	
75	**4b. Give it access to just the `emores` bucket**
76	
77	1. Console → **Cloud Storage** → bucket **emores** → **Permissions** (*Uprawnienia*) tab.
78	2. **Grant access** → New principals: paste the service account email.
79	3. Role: **Storage Object User** (`roles/storage.objectUser`). Save.
80	
81	**4c. Create the key**
82	
83	1. Back in **Service Accounts**, click `github-deploy` → **Keys** tab → **Add key** →
84	   **Create new key** → **JSON** → **Create**.
85	2. A `.json` file downloads. Treat it like a password. Do **not** put it in the project folder.
86	
87	## Step 5 — Give the key to GitHub
88	
89	1. Your repo on GitHub → **Settings** → **Secrets and variables** → **Actions**.
90	2. **New repository secret**.
91	3. Name: `GCP_SA_KEY` (exactly this — the workflow looks for that name).
92	4. Secret: open the downloaded `.json` in a text editor, select all, paste the **entire**
93	   contents including the outer `{ }`.
94	5. **Add secret**. Now delete the `.json` file from your Downloads folder — GitHub has it,
95	   and you can always generate a new one.
96	
97	---
98	
99	## Step 6 — Your day-to-day loop
100	
101	```bash
102	code path/to/emores-site      # or just open the folder in VS Code
103	```
104	
105	Edit `index.html`. When you're happy:
106	
107	- **In VS Code:** Source Control panel (`Ctrl+Shift+G`) → type a short message → **Commit** → **Sync/Push**.
108	- **Or in the terminal:**
109	  ```bash
110	  git add index.html
111	  git commit -m "what I changed"
112	  git push
113	  ```
114	
115	Then open the **Actions** tab on GitHub. You'll see a run appear; green tick = deployed.
116	Refresh your site (`Ctrl+Shift+R` for a hard refresh) and the change is live.
117	
118	To check it went through without GitHub:
119	<https://storage.googleapis.com/emores/index.html>
120	
121	---
122	
123	## Things worth knowing
124	
125	**Caching.** The workflow sets `Cache-Control: no-cache` on `index.html`, so browsers re-check
126	it every time and your edits show up immediately. Without this, GCS defaults to caching HTML
127	for an hour and you'd be staring at a stale page wondering why nothing changed.
128	
129	**Public access is preserved.** Your bucket grants public read at the *bucket* level, so a
130	re-uploaded `index.html` stays publicly readable automatically. Nothing to re-do per upload.
131	
132	**The bucket is still the live copy.** If you ever edit `index.html` directly in the console,
133	your local repo goes out of date — the next push will silently overwrite that console edit.
134	Pick one place to edit (the repo) and stick to it.
135	
136	**Undo a bad deploy.** `git revert HEAD && git push` re-uploads the previous version. If you
137	want belt-and-braces, turn on **Object Versioning** on the bucket so old copies are retained.
138	
139	**Adding more files later.** To also deploy `privacy-policy.txt`, `thumbs/`, etc., add them to
140	the repo and change the upload step in `.github/workflows/deploy.yml` to:
141	
142	```yaml
143	      - name: Sync site to gs://emores
144	        run: |
145	          gcloud storage rsync . gs://emores \
146	            --recursive --exclude='^\.git.*' --cache-control="no-cache, max-age=0"
147	```
148	
149	and widen the `paths:` filter at the top (or remove it).
150	
151	**If the workflow fails**, click the failed run in the Actions tab and open the red step:
152	
153	| Error contains | Fix |
154	| --- | --- |
155	| `credentials_json` / `invalid_grant` | The secret isn't valid JSON — re-paste the whole file contents. |
156	| `403` / `does not have storage.objects.create` | Step 4b didn't take. Re-check the role on the bucket. |
157	| `secrets.GCP_SA_KEY` is empty | Secret name typo, or it was added to the wrong repo. |
158
```

To fix, either:
1. **You already created the repo but under a different name/URL** — go to your GitHub, copy the correct repo URL, then run:

   ```
2. **You haven't created it yet** — go to https://github.com/new, create it (private, no README/gitignore/license), then run the same `set-url` command with the real URL, then `git push -u origin main`.

_**Agent (claude-sonnet-5 2026-08-19 09:56:33Z)**_

If the URL is right, then "Repository not found" almost always means one of these:

1. **The repo doesn't actually exist yet on GitHub** — you created the local repo but haven't hit "Create repository" on github.com yet.
2. **It exists but is private, and your push isn't authenticated** — Git tried the request without valid credentials, and GitHub hides private repos (shows "not found" instead of "403") when you're not authorized.

Let's check your auth situation.

That confirms it: there's no cached GitHub credential in Windows Credential Manager, and my push ran in a non-interactive shell, so Git Credential Manager couldn't pop the browser sign-in window — it just went out unauthenticated. GitHub returns the same generic "Repository not found" for private repos when you're not authenticated, even if `kryptoboi/em` exists and is spelled right.

So this isn't a wrong-URL problem, it's an auth problem, and it needs to happen from an interactive terminal or VS Code (not through me), so the browser sign-in can pop up. Two ways:

**Option A — VS Code (easiest, matches your SETUP.md guide):**
1. Open the `emores-site` folder in VS Code.
2. Source Control icon (`Ctrl+Shift+G`) → **Publish Branch** (or just **Push** since the remote's already set).
3. It'll open a browser to sign into GitHub — sign in as **kryptoboi**.

**Option B — your own terminal:**
```
git push -u origin main
```
run in a normal terminal window (not through me) — GCM should pop the same browser sign-in.

Once you authenticate once, GCM caches it and future pushes (including from me) will just work. Try one of these and let me know if it still fails.

_**Agent (claude-sonnet-5 2026-08-19 09:59:37Z)**_

Since GCM needs a real interactive terminal to pop the browser window, this has to happen outside of me — I can't complete a browser login. Here's how:

**Steps:**
1. Open a normal terminal on your machine (Windows Terminal, or the terminal inside VS Code — `` Ctrl+` ``).
2. Navigate to your repo folder:
   ```
   cd path\to\emores-site
   ```
3. Run:
   ```
   git push -u origin main
   ```
4. A browser window should pop up asking you to sign into GitHub. **Sign in as `kryptoboi`** (the account that owns `github.com/kryptoboi/em`) — not any other GitHub account you might be logged into.
5. Approve/authorize, then the terminal push should complete.

**If no browser window pops up** (sometimes GCM stays silent):
- Force it by clearing any stale cached credential first:
  ```
  git credential-manager github logout
  ```
  then run `git push -u origin main` again.

**Or use VS Code instead**, which is more reliable for this:
- Open the folder in VS Code → Source Control panel (`Ctrl+Shift+G`) → **Publish Branch** (or **Sync Changes**) → it triggers the same browser sign-in as `kryptoboi`.

Once signed in, the credential gets cached in Windows Credential Manager, and every future push (including ones I run for you) will just work without asking again.

Let me know once you've signed in and I'll verify the push went through.
